definitions.meaning: read as a noun, the person who set up and endowed a charity, school or hospital out of generosity
to sink and stick fast, as a horse or cart does in boggy ground

explanation.surface: A dull, conservative person who nonetheless gives generously to good causes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick in the mud' looks like the noun for a dull person, but here it is a verb phrase: to get bogged down. 'Philanthropic' stands for the benefactor who endows an institution.
explanation.definitionFit: A benefactor who endows a charity is remembered by it on its annual day of thanks; a horse that gets bogged down and collapses is said to do the same.

definitions.meaning: someone who loves very hot curries swallows flames, like the circus performer
a quick-tempered, quarrelsome person, ready to pick a fight

explanation.surface: A hot-tempered person who can't get enough curry.
explanation.walkthrough: The circus performer who swallows flames suggests a lover of the hottest curries; the word is also used for a hothead.
explanation.definitionFit: A hothead spoiling for a fight is likened to the circus performer who swallows flames, as is someone who relishes scorching curries.

parts.note: a poetic word, from Latin umbra, shadow, meaning shadowy

explanation.surface: A shady spot where a poet might sit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For the poet' marks a poetic or literary word; it comes from Latin umbra, shade.
explanation.definitionFit: This rare literary adjective comes from Latin for shadow and means darkened or shadowy.

parts.note: the verb for talking a matter over was once used, humorously, for working through a meal

explanation.surface: Someone who chatters on all through dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: To talk something over and, in an old jocular sense, to eat and drink something up ('discuss a bottle') are the same verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to debate or talk over, and in an old humorous use, to consume food or drink with relish.

definitions.meaning: a root of ginger is called by this old word

explanation.surface: A call telling someone nicknamed Ginger to get a move on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ginger' looks like a red-haired person's nickname; it is the root, of which a single piece is so called (Shakespeare's 'a race of ginger').
explanation.definitionFit: To rush is to dash, as in a contest of speed; and an old term for a single root of the spice is the same word.

parts.note: the phrase both tells glum fans to brighten and tells a crowd to start shouting for their side

explanation.surface: Someone urges a disappointed football crowd to keep their spirits up.
explanation.walkthrough: The two-word phrase says 'stop being miserable' and also 'start shouting encouragement', both apt for a losing side's supporters.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a call to be less gloomy, and literally a call to raise a supporting shout, as fans do.

clue.text: Governors find girl-star among the tins!

indicators.note: among says the girl's name goes in the middle of the tins

parts.note: cans are tins
Stella is a girl's name and the Latin word for a star

explanation.surface: Someone discovers a girl who is a star among the food tins.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen in 'girl-star' joins two hints to the same name: a girl's name that is also Latin for 'star'. Castle keepers governed their fortresses, which is why the word looks like 'castle'.
explanation.definitionFit: Keepers of castles were the governors of those fortresses, hence the word's link with 'castle'.

definitions.meaning: ... Gantry is the hypocritical preacher in Sinclair Lewis's 1927 novel of that name
read as an elm with -er added, one who deals in elms

explanation.surface: A gantry is needed to reach the tops for a tree surgeon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gantry' looks like a frame for lifting; it is the surname of Sinclair Lewis's preacher, whose first name is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinclair Lewis's novel names its fraudulent evangelist with this first name, and an elm with -er tacked on gives a fanciful expert in that tree.

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in puts the single letter for one inside the word for no

parts.note: non is Latin and French for no
the Roman numeral I is one

explanation.surface: A puzzled query about a runner who has had one run in.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a quotation: in Macbeth the first witch tells of 'the rump-fed ronyon', a scabby wretch, also spelt this way. 'in' puts I inside NON.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's witch calls a sailor's wife a 'rump-fed' wretch, using this old term of abuse for a mangy woman.

definitions.meaning: ... is Latin for to be able, as in the legal phrase in ..., potentially
a band of men a sheriff summons to help keep the peace

explanation.surface: A group of capable men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Able' looks like an adjective on 'body'; it is the Latin verb meaning 'to be able'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin verb for being able survives in the phrase 'in posse'; a sheriff's band of deputised citizens is the familiar Western sense.

indicators.note: changing means the letters of the archbishop's signature are rearranged

parts.note: the Archbishop of York signs himself Ebor (from Eboracum, Latin for York), plus the S of the possessive

explanation.surface: An archbishop is getting changed out of his clerical dress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Archbishop' gives EBOR, the Latin signature of the Archbishop of York; with the 's it gives EBORS, which 'changing' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Vestments are the ceremonial garments clergy wear, which are long flowing gowns.

parts.note: a quotation to complete from Keats's Ode to a Nightingale, where the magic windows open on perilous seas

explanation.surface: A line from Keats with a word missing for the solver to supply.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats wrote of charmed magic windows opening on the foam of perilous seas in faery lands forlorn; the missing word is a hinged window.

parts.note: the record of a people leaving their land, read as the second book of the Bible, telling of the Israelites leaving Egypt

explanation.surface: A diary kept by people travelling to settle in a new country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Log-book' suggests a ship's journal; it is the Old Testament book recording the Israelites' departure from Egypt.
explanation.definitionFit: The second book of the Old Testament records the Israelites' mass departure from Egypt, so it is the chronicle of a people on the move.

parts.note: on British roads, where traffic keeps left, the left-hand side of a vehicle is the one nearer the kerb

explanation.surface: Someone departed in a typically British manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like 'departed'; it is the left-hand side, which in Britain, driving on the left, is the side next to the pavement.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain the kerbside of a car or horse, the one closer to the pavement, is its left side.

parts.note: a line to complete from Hamlet, Act 1, where Horatio tells Hamlet to temper his wonder at the ghost news

explanation.surface: A line from Hamlet with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Horatio, telling Hamlet of his father's ghost, asks him to restrain his wonder for a while; the dash in the printed clue was lost in scanning.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's line the word means wonder or astonishment, its older sense, which Horatio asks Hamlet to moderate.

parts.note: an American naval term, a force assembled for a particular operation, suggests the work such a force is given

explanation.surface: Duties assigned to the armed forces of the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: The US military term 'task force' lies behind it: such a force is named for the jobs it is formed to do.
explanation.definitionFit: Jobs are pieces of work one is assigned, and a 'task force' is the American military's term for a unit formed for one.

definitions.meaning: hard-working application, as in a person's industry
a public stagecoach, especially in France, a vehicle on wheels

explanation.surface: Manufacturing that runs on wheels, such as the motor trade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Industry' looks like trade or manufacture; it means hard work. The other sense is the French stagecoach.
explanation.definitionFit: Industry in the sense of steady application is careful effort; the old French public stagecoach also bore this name.

parts.note: maggots are grubs, insect larvae
to take is to seize

explanation.surface: Maggots get into a gold prospector's food supplies.
explanation.walkthrough: An American term: supplies or funds given to a prospector in return for a share of what he finds.
explanation.definitionFit: In the American West, backers supplied a miner with food and gear in return for a share of any strike.

parts.note: a word for all people that takes a singular verb, as in 'all of them is here'

explanation.surface: An odd bunch of people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singular' looks like 'odd'; it is the grammar term: this word means all people yet takes a singular verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun covers every person, a whole lot of people, yet is grammatically singular.

clue.text: After being negligent, I get on; so forgiveness, please

parts.note: remiss means careless or negligent in one's duty
taken as written

explanation.surface: A penitent admits carelessness, says they will press on, and asks to be pardoned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After being' sets the order of the pieces; 'get', 'so' and 'please' are padding that turn the clue into a penitent's plea.
explanation.definitionFit: The term is used for the pardoning of sins, as in 'the forgiving of sins' in the Creed.

parts.note: an alley, or ally, is a prized playing ball of glass or alabaster, so the clue names the children's game played with them

explanation.surface: A game played in a back lane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alley' looks like a lane; an alley (or ally) is a prized marble, originally of alabaster.
explanation.definitionFit: Children's games of rolling glass balls use prized ones called alleys, made of alabaster.

clue.text: Universal cinema nude could be improper

parts.note: in British film classification, U marks a film suitable for universal showing

indicators.note: could be says the letters of nude may be arranged in another way

explanation.surface: A film for all audiences showing nudity would be inappropriate.
explanation.walkthrough: U was the British film certificate for universal exhibition. 'could be' rearranges NUDE to NDUE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something excessive or unwarranted is out of place, so the word means inappropriate, as in 'unwarranted influence'.

clue.text: Free indeed as one 26 might be

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as printed (scan agrees): 'Free indeed as one 26 might be'. The only parse is RID in DEED, reading 'indeed' as 'in deed', so 'in' is both the container indicator and part of the leaf for DEED: one word doing two jobs.
annotationWithheld.clue: Free indeed as one 26 might be

definitions.meaning: Samuel Plimsoll gave his name to the load-line mark on ships, so he is the man of the mark
an expert with a rifle, a crack shot

explanation.surface: A tennis player in plimsolls is praised for a good stroke.
explanation.walkthrough: Plimsoll is not the shoe: Samuel Plimsoll was the MP behind the load line painted on ships' hulls, the Plimsoll mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Plimsoll is the man behind a famous line on hulls; a crack shot is an expert at hitting a target.

indicators.note: hearted says the soft letter is put at the heart of the word for man

parts.note: male means a man
p is the music abbreviation for piano, soft

explanation.surface: A gentle man sits up in a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soft-hearted' looks like kind; it says P (piano, soft in music) goes in the heart of MALE.
explanation.definitionFit: A deciduous tree with winged seeds, the source of a sweet syrup, whose leaf is on Canada's flag.

clue.text: Put a word in to thwart?

definitions.text: Put a word in to thwart?

parts.words: Put a word in to thwart
parts.note: the past tense of speak is said to be putting a word in, and putting a wheel rod into someone's wheel blocks them

explanation.surface: Someone interrupts to block a plan.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'to put a spoke in someone's wheel' means to thwart them; the same word is the past tense of speak.
explanation.definitionFit: The past tense of speak means said a word, and to put a wheel-rod in someone's wheel is the idiom for stopping their plans.

clue.text: How the Mad Hatter's bat appeared in the sky ? Wrong!

parts.note: as means in the way that, like

parts.words: the Mad Hatter's bat appeared in the sky
parts.note: in Alice in Wonderland the Hatter sings 'Twinkle, twinkle, little bat... like a tea-tray in the sky'

explanation.surface: A question about the Mad Hatter's song, followed by a cry that the answer is wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hatter's parody of 'Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star' puts the bat up above the world 'like a tea-tray in the sky', so the bat appears AS (a tea) TRAY.
explanation.definitionFit: Going wrong is going off the right path, as in 'led off course'.

clue.text: Work "in maiden meditation — or in Fleet Street

indicators.note: the in that opens the quoted phrase also says the word sits within maiden meditation

explanation.surface: A Shakespeare line about a girl's contemplation, set beside newspaper work.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is from A Midsummer Night's Dream ('In maiden meditation, fancy-free'). Fleet Street was London's newspaper street, where this is the work of preparing copy.
explanation.definitionFit: To prepare written copy for publication by correcting it is the work of a newspaper sub-editor.

definitions.meaning: mocked and exposed to public scorn
set in a wooden frame with holes for head and hands, raised up for public punishment

explanation.surface: Someone mocked after being falsely set up for a crime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frame-up' suggests a false accusation; it is literally the wooden frame of the stocks, raised up on a post.
explanation.definitionFit: Being publicly mocked is a figurative sense of the old punishment of being clamped in a raised wooden frame for crowds to jeer at.

clue.text: One hears things with such frequency

definitions.text: One hears things with such frequency

parts.words: One hears things with such frequency
parts.note: read as a sound wave's frequency within the range the human ear can detect, not as how often

explanation.surface: Someone keeps hearing things over and over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frequency' looks like 'how often'; it is the frequency of sound waves the ear can pick up.
explanation.definitionFit: Frequencies within human hearing, roughly twenty to twenty thousand hertz, are called by this sound-related term.

parts.note: a line to complete from Arthur Hugh Clough's 'Say not the struggle nought availeth', about the light of morning

explanation.surface: A line from Clough's poem with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Clough's poem continues 'When daylight comes, comes in the light'; the missing word names the windows facing the sunrise.
explanation.definitionFit: Windows facing the sunrise are those on the side toward the dawn, the direction of the morning light in Clough's poem.

parts.note: the nursery rhyme Solomon Grundy runs 'born on a Monday, christened on' the next day of the week

explanation.surface: A family named Grundy plans when to christen a baby.
explanation.walkthrough: Solomon Grundy is the English nursery-rhyme figure whose whole life passes in one week, christened the day after his Monday birth.
explanation.definitionFit: In the nursery rhyme, Solomon Grundy is christened the day after his Monday birth, the second day of the week.
